cards.title: US, China, Russia sign ‘peace declaration’ after historic Trump, Xi, Putin meeting
cards.author: AFP
cards.why: A historic trilateral summit between major global powers with direct implications for global strategic stability and UN reform.
cards.summary: Leaders of China, the United States, and Russia issued a joint Declaration toward Peace following a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen. The summit brought together Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin to discuss international security and nuclear risk management. The three leaders agreed on plans to overhaul the United Nations and check the International Criminal Court. They also reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
key_facts: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for an 80-minute summit at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen.
The three leaders issued a trilateral document titled Declaration toward Peace.
The declaration reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
The leaders agreed to work on overhauling the United Nations and keeping the International Criminal Court (ICC) in check.
Discussions also included boosting the production and supply of refined petroleum products.

vocab.meaning: rapid increase or spread, especially of nuclear weapons
a collection of weapons and military equipment

text: China, the United States and Russia issued a “Declaration toward Peace” on Thursday after their leaders held an unprecedented summit, laying out common ambitions to overhaul the UN and keep the International Criminal Court (ICC) in check.

The statement, issued after Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in China, said they wanted to protect diplomatic immunity for state officials and also boost supply and production of refined petroleum products.

“The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security,” a White House version of the statement said.

“The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.”
Beijing has long maintained that the United States and Russia must reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its smaller stockpile.
The huddle took place with Russia’s years-long offensive in Ukraine grinding on, Trump bogged down in the Middle East , and an ascendant China looking to strengthen its hand in East Asia.

“We discussed the question of democracy. And what is democracy? It’s what? It’s the liberal order that certain circles put together and still now are trying to impose on the whole world,” Putin told a news conference in Shenzhen.
The three men made opening remarks touching on weighty topics from nuclear weapons to the war in Ukraine as they met around a large, dark round table with a pink flower arrangement at its centre.
The discussion behind closed doors in Kylin Villa ended after an hour and 20 minutes.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting before journalists were sent away.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
“The three countries share a common perspective on safeguarding world peace,” Xi said, while Putin said they wrote a new “page in the history of diplomacy”.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
“It’s not an easy thing to do, give them up,” Trump told Xi and Putin as the meeting began.
None of the presidents made immediate statements after their meeting, and Trump departed on his flight back to the US.
ICC, UN and oil

In their joint statement, the leaders “recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction”.
Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant, while Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.
The leaders said they were “committed to reform the UN so that the UN can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security”.

The joint statement said the countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows”.
The summit stoked fears that the three powerful men want to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions impacting Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.
Differences over Ukraine, Iran and trade
Earlier on Thursday, Trump and Putin held a meeting — their first since August 2025 — with the 80-year-old US president calling the Russian his “friend”.
Putin responded in English: “Nice to meet you.”
Trump and Xi then came together — their third time this year — for one-on-one discussions, with the US leader highlighting a “very special relationship”.
Putin, 74, and Xi, 73, held talks on Wednesday — their 50th meeting, the Chinese president said.

Trump and Xi met after an extension of their trade truce this month, but also amid growing tension over reports of Nvidia chips being diverted to China through Southeast Asia, raising questions about the effectiveness of US export curbs and the future of Chinese access to advanced technology.

The three countries have deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. Their meeting, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.

Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries had “numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine”.

Unlike Trump and Putin, Xi did not make a direct reference to Ukraine, but said: “History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil.”
Trump said both he and Xi felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been disrupted by the Iran war.
Xi did not directly mention Iran in any of his remarks.
“China, Russia, and the United States should continue encouraging parties to conflicts to sit down and engage in talks, and resolve disputes through political and diplomatic means,” Xi said.

The Kylin Villa where they met has a long history of sensitive diplomatic encounters. Its past visitors include former North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, Xi’s father Xi Zhongxun, and envoys of the Dalai Lama.
Airport welcome
Breaking with decades of diplomatic protocol, Xi received Trump at the airport, with the men briefly hugging before a red-carpet greeting complete with cheering children and an air-force flyover.
This reciprocated the airport greeting Trump gave Xi at Joint Base Andrews in September.
“It’s a friendship relationship. It’s a respect relationship,” Trump told Fox News.
The airport welcome showed “great respect, and I appreciate that. That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too,” Trump said.
Other world leaders at the Apec meeting included Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, South Korea’s Lee Jae Myung, Canada’s Mark Carney and Australia’s Anthony Albanese.
Takaichi, on her first visit since angering Beijing a year ago with comments about Taiwan, met Putin — relations are also tense — on Wednesday, Tokyo said.
Takaichi, who by Thursday afternoon had not held any formal meeting with Xi, said on Thursday she wanted a “constructive and stable relationship” with China.
Despite their differences, all the leaders — including Putin — posed for the Apec “family photo” on Thursday in special scarves.
Xi opened the Apec leaders’ meeting on Thursday with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.

cards.title: Top UN court finds Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against Muslim Rohingya
cards.author: Reuters
cards.why: A landmark verdict in international law establishing state responsibility under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
cards.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar's military committed state-sponsored genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017. Presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa delivered the landmark decision in a lawsuit filed seven years earlier by Gambia. The judges found the military responsible for systematic mass killings, widespread sexual violence, and destroying hundreds of villages. This marks the first time the World Court has held an entire state legally responsible for genocide.
key_facts: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) found the Republic of the Union of Myanmar guilty of state-sponsored genocide in Northern Rakhine State.
The case was instituted at the ICJ seven years prior by predominantly Muslim Gambia.
The decision is the first time an international court held a state directly responsible for genocide.
The ruling delivered by presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa is final and cannot be appealed.

vocab.meaning: the deliberate killing of a large number of people from a particular nation or ethnic group
completely destroyed or flattened to the ground

text: The highest United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met.
It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya,” presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.
The panel found “that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State.”
Myanmar’s government did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.
Decision is expected to influence other genocide cases

Judges found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations.
The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
Genocide has rarely been established in international courts, largely because prosecutors must prove a specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The decision by the International Court of Justice, or World Court, is expected to have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, including for South Africa’s 2023 case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza .

The first major decision by the court in more than a decade on the application of the 1948 Genocide Convention will be pored over by legal experts for clues to how the bench assessed state responsibility in the alleged commission of international crimes.
Both Israel and Myanmar deny genocide and say their forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups.
In a major legal victory for Gambia, the court found the state responsible for genocide resulting from a military offensive that drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

A panel of 15 judges said “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state,” meeting the legal threshold for genocide.
The court said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.
Myanmar must also allow the “safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts,” it said.
International courts previously only recognised genocide during the 1994 Rwanda genocide , the 1995 Srebrenica killings in Bosnia, and atrocities by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s.
While rulings by the ICJ, which settles disputes between states and rules on alleged breaches of international treaties, are final, the court has very limited options to enforce them.
It is distinct from the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against ​humanity and genocide and can impose jail terms.

cards.title: FCC sets aside high court rulings upholding infrastructure cess in Sindh, KP
cards.author: Nasir Iqbal
cards.why: Clarifies constitutional limits on provincial taxation and the division of fiscal powers between the federation and provinces.
cards.summary: The Federal Constitutional Court set aside high court decisions that had previously upheld provincial infrastructure cesses in Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. A two-judge bench reviewed 568 petitions contesting the provincial taxes on goods and trade. The court examined constitutional boundaries regarding provincial taxation on foreign trade and inter-provincial goods movement. The dispute centered on laws enacted by Sindh in 2017 and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2022.
key_facts: A two-judge bench of the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) headed by Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan and Justice Aamer Farooq set aside high court rulings on provincial infrastructure cesses.
The case addressed 568 petitions challenging the Sindh Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2017 and the KP Infrastructure Development Cess Act, 2022.
Section 14 of the KP Finance Act, 2024 had raised the provincial cess from one percent to two percent.
The legal dispute originated in Sindh in 1994 before being formalized through provincial legislation in 2017.

vocab.meaning: a tax or levy imposed for a specific purpose
related directly to or concerned a specific matter

text: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Thursday set aside high court rulings upholding the infrastructure cess imposed by the Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governments.

The case pertained to the Sindh Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2017 and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Infrastructure Development Cess Act, 2022, including amendments introduced through the KP Finance Act, 2024.

Headed by FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan, a two-judge bench, also comprising Justice Aamer Farooq, had taken up a batch of 568 petitions by private petitioners challenging decisions by the Sindh High Court (SHC) and the Peshawar High Court (PHC) upholding the cesses.
The FCC bench examined the constitutional limits of provincial taxation in relation to imports, exports, customs-related transactions and the movement of goods across provincial boundaries.

The Sindh infrastructure cess controversy originated in 1994 and was subsequently governed by the Sindh Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2017, which provided for taxes on goods entering or leaving Sindh from or for outside the country through air or sea. On June 4, 2021, the SHC upheld the levy.

Similarly, the KP Infrastructure Development Cess Act, 2022, imposed cess on the transportation and movement of goods in the province. Section 14 of the KP Finance Act, 2024, amended Section 3 of the 2022 Act to enhance the cess rate from one to two per cent. The PHC, through its Nov 14, 2025 judgement, dismissed 157 petitions challenging the levy and upheld its legality.

The judgements of both high courts were subsequently challenged before the FCC. The petitioners argued that the provinces lacked constitutional authority to impose fiscal levies on imports, exports and goods falling within the federal legislative domain.

They maintained that the impugned laws encroached upon Parliament’s exclusive legislative competence. Consequently, the provincial provisions and the high court judgements upholding them could not be sustained.

Senior counsel Hafiz Ehsaan Ahmad Khokhar, while representing the secretary of the Revenue Division and the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), submitted that the impugned provincial levies had to be examined in the light of Articles 141 and 142(a) of the Constitution, read with Entries 27, 43 and 59 of Part I of the Federal Legislative List (FLL) in the Fourth Schedule.

He explained that Entry 27 covered imports and exports across customs frontiers, inter-provincial trade and commerce and trade with foreign countries, whereas Entry 43 specifically assigned customs duties, including export duties, to the federation.
The counsel contended that under Article 142(a), Parliament had exclusive legislative competence over matters enumerated in the FLL.

The constitutional character of a levy, he argued, must be determined by its true nature, taxable event, fiscal incidence, charging provisions and actual operation, not merely by its nomenclature as an infrastructure cess.
A provincial levy imposing an additional fiscal burden on imported or exported goods and operating through the customs-clearance mechanism directly engaged the federal legislative domain, he said.

He also referred to Article 163, explaining that the provincial power to impose taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments could not be extended to customs duties or other subjects constitutionally assigned to the Parliament.
The counsel further argued that a provincial legislature could not acquire legislative competence over a federal subject merely by describing a customs-linked fiscal levy as an infrastructure cess.
Meanwhile, the Sindh and KP governments defended their respective laws, arguing that the taxes were provincial levies intended to finance infrastructure development and road facilities.

They maintained that it was not a customs or export duty and that the provincial assemblies were competent to legislate on such matters under Article 142(c) of the Constitution and the impugned judgements were legal.
The additional attorney general supported the federation’s position, submitting that the provincial governments lacked legislative competence to impose levies falling within the FLL.
After hearing the arguments, the FCC set aside the two high court judgements and declared that the legislations were beyond the legislative competence of the provinces.

cards.title: COP31 negotiators publish revised deal draft with no mention of fossil fuels
cards.author: Reuters
cards.why: Illustrates key divisions in global climate diplomacy regarding fossil fuel phase-out and international adaptation finance.
cards.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 summit in Antalya removed language calling for an end to fossil fuels from a revised draft agreement. The updated text also dropped a proposed target of 120 billion dollars in adaptation funding for developing economies. The draft still acknowledged that global warming could exceed the critical 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold. Developing country advocates criticized the changes, warning the meeting risks failing to deliver meaningful outcomes.
key_facts: The COP31 climate conference took place in Antalya, Turkiye, under a split presidency with Australia.
The revised text stripped out references to limiting or ending fossil fuel usage.
Negotiators removed a proposed 120 billion dollar adaptation finance target intended for developing countries.
The draft retained an acknowledgement that global temperature increases may exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit.

vocab.meaning: a level or point at which a new status or reaction begins
adjustments in ecological, social, or economic systems to lessen climate change damage

text: Climate negotiators stripped out any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels in a slimmed-down draft deal text published on Thursday, as the COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkiye, approaches its Friday deadline.

The talks are taking place at a time when war and rising living costs are competing for the attention of policymakers and the public against the warming climate and its increasingly severe effects, including heatwaves, floods and droughts.

The revised deal, which is not expected to be the final version, was weaker on some of the conference’s central topics — fossil fuels, electrification and adaptation finance — compared to a first draft published on Monday.

Monday’s two references to fossil fuels and limiting their use a topic that deeply divides nations in the negotiations every year — were removed, as was mention of a $120 billion target for finance to help developing countries adapt to climate change.
“This new text has gone backwards from the one released earlier in the week,” said Mohamed Adow, director of climate and energy think tank Power Shift Africa.
“If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”

Thursday’s draft did retain an acknowledgement that global warming could exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold countries have sought to preserve, and the need for “deep, rapid and sustained” cuts to greenhouse gas emissions.
It also encouraged efforts to scale up the deployment of technologies that can suck carbon out of the atmosphere, something scientists say would be needed to bring temperatures back down.
Start broad and narrow down

Australia, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement with Turkiye, previously said Monday’s opening draft of the deal was always intended to be a broad document that would then be narrowed down.

While the conference is scheduled to end on Friday, in recent years efforts to secure consensus among the nearly 200 countries participating have regularly blown past this deadline by more than 24 hours.
The need to limit rising global temperatures is widely accepted by participants, but they don’t all agree on the best way to do so, who should pay for it, and how quickly the world needs to act.

Thursday’s draft deal also called for “global cooperation” to boost electricity’s share of world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, up from around 23pc now — something proponents say would slash greenhouse gas emissions by reducing fossil fuel use.
The previous draft had more firmly set that as a target but came up against resistance from developing nations that argued it would require significant funding.
The so-called 35-by-35 goal had been put forward by COP host Turkiye, but so far only about 75 nations have backed it.
Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation, said the electrification goal wasn’t clear enough on how the target would accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.
He also said the mention of carbon removal technologies opened the door to the fossil fuel industry to keep ramping up production.
“Anything that provides a way for the fossil fuel industry to keep polluting the climate would be a profound backwards step at a time when climate impacts are rapidly worsening,” he said.

cards.title: Turkish energy minister arrives in Karachi ahead of Oruç Reis offshore exploration mission
cards.author: Web Desk
cards.why: A significant step for Pakistan's energy security and offshore resource exploration through bilateral cooperation with Turkiye.
cards.summary: Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar arrived in Karachi to oversee the arrival of the seismic research vessel Oruc Reis. The vessel will conduct offshore oil and gas exploration in Pakistani waters. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik welcomed the delegation and noted this mission marks the first major offshore survey in Pakistan in two decades. The project represents a deepening of bilateral energy cooperation between Pakistan and Turkiye.
key_facts: Turkish seismic research vessel Oruç Reis was deployed to conduct offshore oil and gas exploration in Pakistan.
The mission marks the revival of offshore oil and gas exploration activities in Pakistan after 20 years.
Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar was received in Karachi by Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik.

vocab.meaning: relating to earth vibrations used to map underground and undersea geological formations

cards.title: DPM Dar, Asean secretary general agree to enhance cooperation to address ‘non-traditional’ security challenges
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: Reflects Pakistan's diplomatic pivot toward Southeast Asia and joint action on non-traditional security challenges.
cards.summary: Pakistan and ASEAN agreed to expand cooperation to manage non-traditional security challenges during talks in Islamabad. Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and ASEAN Secretary General Dr Kao Kim Hourn led the discussions. The dialogue prioritized threats involving climate change, food insecurity, disrupted energy supplies, and cyber vulnerabilities. Both sides also agreed to build stronger university linkages in digital technologies and artificial intelligence.
key_facts: Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar held delegation-level talks in Islamabad with ASEAN Secretary General Dr Kao Kim Hourn.
Cooperation was pledged on non-traditional security challenges including food security, cyber threats, climate change, and energy disruptions.
The sides agreed to establish institutional links between universities in digital technologies and artificial intelligence.

vocab.meaning: a brief public briefing or press conference

cards.title: Pakistan, 14 other countries welcome UK, Australia sanctions on Israeli 'settlement activities'
cards.author: Web Desk
cards.why: Demonstrates coordinated multilateral diplomatic action supporting Palestinian sovereignty and opposing illegal settlement expansion.
cards.summary: Pakistan and fourteen other nations welcomed sanctions imposed by the United Kingdom and Australia on Israeli settlement operations. The measures target construction firms building settlements across the occupied West Bank. British sanctions focused on companies participating in the controversial E1 project, which divides the West Bank and separates it from East Jerusalem. Australia also placed penalties on individuals and entities linked to human rights abuses in Palestinian territory.
key_facts: Pakistan and 14 other nations, including Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, and Turkiye, issued a joint statement welcoming UK and Australian sanctions.
The UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies building settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Sanctions came ahead of deadlines for the E1 settlement project, which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
Australia sanctioned three individuals and four entities involved in West Bank settlement expansion.

vocab.meaning: to divide or cut into two separate parts
encouraging or helping someone to commit an illegal act
